constraints: Read-only permissions are part of the first-release scope.
Evidence checks and escalation are executable.
The partner needs reproducible schemas, tests, and recovery guidance.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the partner needed only a non-operational visual overview with no tools or side effects, a runbook could be reduced to interface links.
details.errorCorrection: Vague qualities, write credentials, happy-path examples, and partner discretion omit the explicit scope and executable procedure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic stresses transparency, documented tool interfaces, ground truth from tool results, and thorough testing for reliable agent systems.
details.scenarioApplication: Show the invoice and ledger data flow, enforce read-only tools, specify insufficient-evidence stops, and give the partner schemas, tests, deployment, and recovery steps.
details.transfer: Document negative permission boundaries and the executable runbook needed to reproduce and operate them.

messages.text: Model qualities do not define permissions, evidence thresholds, or escalation behavior.
Write access violates the first-release boundary and creates an unnecessary ledger side effect.
A happy path does not specify insufficient evidence or recovery.
The data-flow record makes read-only scope and evidence stops visible to the implementer.
A versioned runbook makes schemas, checks, deployment, and recovery reproducible.

feedback.reason: The handoff must preserve the no-write scope and make the implementation and operations procedure reproducible for the partner.

options.text: List model qualities and tell the partner to use good judgment when evidence is uncertain.
Provide a boundary-focused architecture and data-flow record showing read-only permissions and evidence stops.
Give the partner write credentials so it can validate matches against the ledger during implementation.
Document only the happy-path invoice example and let the partner choose the escalation behavior.
Supply a versioned runbook with schemas, traces, acceptance checks, deployment, and recovery steps.

prompt: A reconciliation agent reads invoices and a ledger, proposes a match, and pauses when evidence is insufficient; an external partner must implement it without ledger writes in the first release. Select TWO handoff controls.

constraints: The prototype and architect can be inspected.
Customer fields have different access permissions.
The receiving team needs a testable production contract.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the framework already exposed versioned schemas, permissions, traces, and acceptance tests, the page could link to those canonical interfaces.
details.errorCorrection: Terminology and successful anecdotes do not define a contract, and deferring or delegating permissions creates inconsistent high-impact behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends tool definitions with clear formats, boundaries, examples, edge cases, and testing alongside transparent agent design.
details.scenarioApplication: Document field-level access, tool input/output schemas, approval and stop conditions, acceptance checks, examples, and failure escalation before handoff.
details.transfer: Replace vague architecture prose with explicit interfaces, permissions, controls, examples, tests, and failure paths.

messages.text: Vocabulary and a successful trace do not define field access, tool input/output, or stopping behavior.
Waiting shifts a foreseeable data and side-effect gap into production and makes teams diverge.
Per-deployment permission choices remove a consistent security and acceptance boundary.

feedback.reason: The page omits the contracts an implementer and reviewer need; replacing it with explicit data, tool, side-effect, and acceptance boundaries makes behavior testable.

options.text: Replace the vague page with a decision/interface record for field permissions, tool schemas, approval and stops, checks, examples, and failure paths.
Add framework vocabulary, a successful trace, and an implementation owner, then let the team infer permissions and stopping rules.
Defer the contract until production shows which fields and tools are used, then document the observed behavior in the next revision.
Add a careful-use instruction and let each implementer choose field permissions and approval handling for its deployment.

prompt: An architecture page says “use an agent framework and retrieve customer history” but omits field permissions, tool I/O, human approval, stopping, and success checks. What documentation repair is needed?

constraints: Prototype traces and approval policy establish allowed data and tools.
Non-goals and stopping conditions can be written into the guide.
Each unresolved assumption needs an accountable owner.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the guide already versioned non-goals, permissions, and approval conditions and the partner passed acceptance, a diagram update could be enough.
details.errorCorrection: General judgment, a later security review, or staging writes leave authority ambiguous and test the wrong scope.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends clearly documented tool boundaries, formats, edge cases, and testing so agent behavior remains transparent and controlled; the non-goal and ownership rules are scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Reconcile the guide with traces and approval policy, remove write authority, document prohibited side effects and stops, assign assumption owners, and make escalation mandatory for any scope change.
details.transfer: Make negative scope, assumption ownership, and escalation explicit in every cross-team agent handoff.

messages.text: A caution does not enforce the out-of-scope boundary or define a permitted future use.
Late security review leaves scope and accountable assumptions unresolved while implementation proceeds.
Staging writes normalize an unapproved side effect before the first-release contract is agreed.

feedback.reason: An out-of-scope write must be removed and named as a negative boundary; assumptions and expansion authority need owners before implementation proceeds.

options.text: Keep the write tool in the guide, restrict it by a caution, and review unusual partner actions during the pilot.
Leave scope implicit and let partner security review decide write eligibility after implementation.
Remove the write tool, record the non-goal, assign assumption owners, and require escalation before scope expands.
Allow writes in staging, collect traces, and decide production scope after the partner completes its happy-path test.

prompt: A partner implements a diagram-heavy agent guide and adds a write tool that the original team considered out of scope; the guide has no explicit non-goals, assumption owner, or failure/escalation contract. What should the owner do?

constraints: The architecture record, tool schema, deployed permissions, runbook version, and acceptance tests can be compared; no write operation has been approved.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the write capability were explicitly approved, documented, and covered by acceptance and rollback, the handoff could version that expanded contract rather than remove it.
details.errorCorrection: The write authority was not approved, and treating deployment as authority converts an unreviewed side effect into the contract by accident. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends tool definitions with clear formats, boundaries, examples, edge cases, and testing, alongside transparent agent design. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Disable or remove the unauthorized write path, reconcile the architecture, schema, permissions, runbook, and acceptance tests to one versioned source, then rerun conformance checks before handoff.
details.transfer: Stop a handoff at a side-effect mismatch and reconcile every executable artifact to one owned contract.

messages.text: Deployment is not authority for an unapproved side effect, and a later runbook update would normalize it accidentally.
Staging still exercises the out-of-scope permission and makes the wrong contract appear accepted.
A documented discrepancy without a conformance decision leaves the partner unable to know which boundary is canonical.
Required control: Disable or remove the unauthorized write path before the partner exercises the workflow.
Required control: Reconcile the architecture, tool schema, permissions, runbook, and acceptance tests to one versioned source, then rerun conformance checks.

feedback.reason: Disable or remove the unauthorized write path, reconcile the architecture, schema, permissions, runbook, and acceptance tests to one versioned source, then rerun conformance checks before handoff. The decisive constraint is Documentation and implementation disagree on a side-effect boundary; the handoff must stop and reconcile the authoritative contract before any write capability is exercised.

options.text: Disable or remove the unauthorized write path before the partner exercises the workflow.
Keep the write tool because deployment is the most current artifact and update the runbook after partner validation.
Permit the write in staging and decide its production status after the partner completes the happy path.
Reconcile the architecture, tool schema, permissions, runbook, and acceptance tests to one versioned source, then rerun conformance checks.
Document the discrepancy as a known exception and proceed with the deployed configuration while no write is requested.

prompt: A partner’s implementation grants a write tool, while the canonical architecture and current runbook describe a read-only workflow. The partner asks whether the diagram or the deployed configuration should be treated as authoritative. Select TWO: Which actions resolve the handoff disagreement?

constraints: The current guide, tool schemas, operator permissions, sample requests/responses, failure fixtures, and owner contacts are available; the operator has no access to developer internals.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the guide already used operator-visible contracts, examples, permissions, failure actions, and a passing dry run, the existing versioned handoff could be accepted.
details.errorCorrection: Inference at incident time can cross permissions or side-effect boundaries, and a late contact does not test whether the operator can recover safely. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends tool definitions with clear formats, boundaries, examples, edge cases, and testing, alongside transparent agent design. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Rewrite the guide around operator-visible inputs/outputs, preconditions, examples, stop and escalation actions, and recovery ownership, then run a partner dry run against failure fixtures before sign-off.
details.transfer: Write handoffs for the operator who must act at the boundary, then exercise recovery before declaring the phase complete.

messages.text: Inferring commands at incident time can cross permissions and side-effect boundaries; a late contact is not a recovery test.
A happy path does not tell the operator when to stop or how to recover safely.
Shorter labels do not make the missing contract, owner, or failure action executable.
Required control: Rewrite the guide around operator-visible inputs, outputs, preconditions, examples, stop actions, escalation, and recovery ownership.
Required control: Run a partner dry run against failure fixtures before sign-off and record the named handoff and recovery owners.

feedback.reason: Rewrite the guide around operator-visible inputs/outputs, preconditions, examples, stop and escalation actions, and recovery ownership, then run a partner dry run against failure fixtures before sign-off. The decisive constraint is An implementation-ready handoff must be executable by its audience at the documented boundary; developer-only vocabulary and a happy path do not provide a safe operator recovery contract.

options.text: Send the diagram and ask the operator to infer commands from source code, then add a support contact after the first incident.
Rewrite the guide around operator-visible inputs, outputs, preconditions, examples, stop actions, escalation, and recovery ownership.
Keep the happy-path guide and let the operator ask the developer team for recovery steps when a failure occurs.
Replace the internal class names with shorter labels but leave permissions, failure actions, and escalation implicit.
Run a partner dry run against failure fixtures before sign-off and record the named handoff and recovery owners.

prompt: An external operator must run a claims workflow, but the handoff guide uses internal class names and diagram arrows without concrete inputs, outputs, preconditions, failure actions, or an escalation contact. The implementation passes the developer happy path. Select TWO: Which controls make this handoff executable?

constraints: The receiving team needs both implementation and operations guidance.
Approval and account-change boundaries must remain explicit.
Evaluation and recovery evidence are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the receiving team already owned the same interfaces and runbook, a focused model/configuration change note could suffice.
details.errorCorrection: A model, prompt, screenshot, or dependency list omits permissions, checks, approval timing, and failure handling; documenting after a write is too late.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says agents need ground truth, human checkpoints or stopping conditions, and clearly documented tools to remain controlled and reliable.
details.scenarioApplication: Version the data flow, tool schemas, retrieved evidence, recommendation and approval contract, tests, deployment settings, and incident/recovery steps.
details.transfer: Handoff documentation should let another team reproduce, operate, verify, and safely stop the workflow.

messages.text: Examples help, but inference leaves account-change authority, evaluation, and recovery undocumented.
Dependencies and a trace do not set field permissions, tool contracts, approval, or incident ownership for operations.
Post-change documentation cannot protect the first side effect or give operators a tested recovery path.

feedback.reason: The handoff must preserve interfaces and operational and safety boundaries, not just demonstrate one successful output.

options.text: Send model name, prompt, screenshot, data-flow notes, and a successful trace, then let operators infer approval and recovery.
Hand over a versioned architecture diagram and runbook for data/tools, contracts, approval, tests, configuration, and recovery.
Provide dependencies and a prototype trace, leaving permission and incident behavior to the receiving team’s implementation plan.
Share prompt and deployment command, document approval after the first account change, and update the runbook after operations begin.

prompt: A claims-processing workflow retrieves policy text, drafts a recommendation, and requires approval before an account change; another team must implement and operate it. What handoff package is needed?

constraints: The partner needs a safe validation step.
The guide is a release interface, not a static overview.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the model and schema were pinned and no context behavior changed, a release note could supplement an unchanged guide.
details.errorCorrection: Release notes do not update parser assumptions, a permanent pin blocks justified change, and larger limits can worsen mismatch rather than repair schema.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says agent implementations should be measured and iterated while preserving simplicity, transparency, and documented tool interfaces.
details.scenarioApplication: Update model and context assumptions, schema examples, truncation checks, parser tests, owner responsibilities, and the partner’s staging validation before cutover.
details.transfer: Treat handoff guidance as a versioned interface and require downstream validation whenever runtime contracts change.

messages.text: A disclaimer and post-deployment comparison do not update the executable parser contract or prove safe compatibility.
Pinning avoids the mismatch temporarily but blocks a managed transition from the retired contract.
Capacity changes cannot repair a schema mismatch or define a release validation step.

feedback.reason: The guide must track the runtime contract and give the partner a validation gate; a disclaimer or permanent pin does not repair executable assumptions.

options.text: Add a disclaimer to the old guide, publish release notes, and ask the partner to compare parser errors after deployment.
Pin the old model and parser until the partner can schedule a migration window for a future contract change.
Version model, context, and schema contracts, update examples and regression checks, and require partner validation before release.
Increase context and output limits, preserve the old parser, and monitor rejected responses during the release.

prompt: A model update changes context limits and output schema, but the partner’s guide still describes the old contract; evidence is truncated and a downstream parser rejects responses. What should happen before the next release?
